query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy with an FCC matrix, degradation at high temperature is primarily governed by the selective oxidation of the reactive elements (Al and Ti) in an oxidizing environment. This oxidation produces a brittle oxide scale that, due to thermal expansion mismatch with the underlying matrix, concentrates stresses at grain boundaries and leads to crack initiation and propagation, ultimately causing catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: Freshly additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with a uniform FCC matrix and minimal pre-existing oxide phases.
generation.intervention: Expose samples to controlled high-temperature environments while switching the gas atmosphere from oxidizing (e.g., air or oxygen-rich) to reducing (e.g., hydrogen-containing) conditions.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures above approximately 700°C maintained for extended periods in either oxidizing or reducing atmospheres.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and growth of brittle oxide scales (rich in Al- and Ti-oxides) along the alloy surface and at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Under oxidizing conditions, reactive elements oxidize to form a brittle scale with a different coefficient of thermal expansion than the alloy matrix. This mismatch induces stresses that lead to cracking, particularly along grain boundaries, causing a loss in mechanical integrity. In a reducing atmosphere, oxide formation is suppressed, thereby maintaining grain boundary cohesion and delaying or reducing catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under oxidizing conditions, observable oxide buildup, increased micro-cracking (particularly along grain boundaries), and a significant decline in mechanical properties relative to the baseline; under reducing conditions, slower or minimal oxide growth and retention of higher mechanical integrity.
generation.baseline: The initial microstructure and mechanical performance of the as-manufactured alloy without significant oxidation.
generation.boundary: High-temperature exposures above ~700°C in either oxidizing or reducing atmospheres over durations sufficient to promote surface scale development.
generation.uncertainty: Exact temperature thresholds, oxidation kinetics, and the detailed oxide phase compositions remain uncertain; further quantitative experiments are necessary to refine these parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of identical alloy specimens and subject them to high-temperature exposures (e.g., 750°C) in two controlled environments: one oxidizing (air or oxygen-rich) and one reducing (e.g., hydrogen mixed with inert gas). Monitor the specimens over time using surface analysis (SEM, EDS) to measure oxide scale thickness and crack formation, and conduct mechanical testing (tensile or bending tests) to assess changes in strength.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and composition (via SEM/EDS or XRD)
Crack density and distribution (using optical or electron microscopy)
Mechanical strength and ductility (via tensile or bending tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if, in the oxidizing condition, there is no significant increase in oxide scale formation, corresponding thermal mismatch-induced cracking, or reduction in mechanical performance relative to the reducing condition and baseline. Alternatively, if a similar degradation pattern is observed regardless of the gas environment, or if an entirely different degradation mechanism (e.g., vacancy coalescence without oxidation influence) dominates, the hypothesis would be considered contradictory.
